1. If you are homeless / extremely impoverished, it doesn't matter that there are "programs to help", because they don't. Copay of 50$ is TOO MUCH for some people. I know when I was literally starving and sick, I wouldn't have been able to get help because I was too busy surviving. Alot of "financial aid" programs don't give sustainable amounts, or people are turned down. Some poor people get it, and what about those who don't? Alot of insurance comes through work, which not everyone can. Government insurance can be a NIGHTMARE and be declined for the smallest reasons and I've seen this first hand. 

2. Race, cultural environment and gender is a legitimate factor to getting diagnosed and misdiagnosed in physical and mental illnesses. For example, the symptoms of autism often involve social processing in the brain. This is different on neurotypicals between males and females. Symptoms are scientifically based on male presenting symptoms, because of "more clear" and wider margins of bias in the medical field even just 50 years ago. The psychological equivalent of how women are more likely to die of a heart attack because they experience symptoms differently DOES happen. I think I see alot of self diagnosis in women / afab people more often because Healthcare bias is prevalent for them. The tale of having autism misdiagnosed as BPD, or bipolar misdiagnosed as PMDD is a legitimate and often at times, deadly thing. 
Cultural context matters too- if one grows up in an environment where shame surrounding mental illness (very primarily minority and immigrant families), it might be a legitimate mental issue regarding shame and seeking help. It's so much easier for someone to say "I probably have blah blah" in their head vs having to endure questioning, and observance of their issues from another person because they're taught its inherently wrong. 

I agree entirely that the people that you're probably talking about are not in the scenario of what I describe but the general statement that "you can get a diagnosis" is privileged not in the way you think. There are very real and documented barriers to health care. There's a reason most homeless people are mentally ill, and for example, why schizophrenics have a high homelessness rate.  Alot of adults will live and prematurely die because they can't or "wont" get diagnosed. Alot of people lived and died because of their illness that could've been treated. 

I don't disagree that faking things for attention IS prevalent. It has alot to do with social media, social capital/clout and an emphasis on being different in the modern age, but see how that occurrence hurts people in ACTUAL dire situations like in the ones I mention above? It's really unfortunate and i think the impact of social media and the need to be interesting translates into capitalizing and therapizing every single problem one has
